lesson.title: Why the Absolute Value Matters: The Integral of 1/x
lesson.summary: The antiderivative of 1/x is the natural log of the absolute value of x, not just ln(x), because 1/x is defined for negative numbers while ln(x) alone is not.
lesson.body:
The integral of 1/x is: integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C, valid for all x not equal to 0.

For positive x, this rule is a direct readout of the derivative of ln(x), a listed building block for this chapter: the derivative of ln(x) is 1/x. Running that fact backward, integral of (1/x) dx = ln(x) + C, at least when x is positive, since ln(x) itself is only defined there.

The trouble is that 1/x is a perfectly good, well defined number when x is negative. For example, at x = -2, 1/x = -1/2, no problem at all. But ln(x) is undefined for negative inputs, since no real power of e produces a negative number. So the simple antiderivative ln(x) cannot be the whole story, an antiderivative valid on the negative numbers is still needed.

The absolute value fixes this gap. For negative x, |x| = -x, so ln|x| = ln(-x). Differentiating this with the chain rule gives d/dx[ln(-x)] = (1/(-x)) * (-1), and the two negative signs cancel, leaving 1/x. So the derivative of ln|x| equals 1/x for negative x, exactly matching the integrand, just as it does for positive x. That is why the general rule is written with the absolute value, integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C, covering both sides of the domain in a single formula.

One domain note worth keeping in mind: x = 0 itself is always excluded, since 1/x is undefined there and ln|x| has no value at 0 either, so the rule only makes sense on an interval that stays entirely positive or entirely negative.

Worked example: find integral of (4/x) dx. Using the constant multiple rule, pull the 4 outside: 4 * integral of (1/x) dx = 4*ln|x| + C. Verify by differentiating: the derivative of 4*ln|x| is 4*(1/x) = 4/x, which matches the original integrand.
